name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,135

clue.text: Having layers aids fitter when working

indicators.note: something working is in operation and moving about, so the letters are set in motion into a new order

blocks.note: the ten letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A tradesman's helpers turn up in several layers of work clothes while on the job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Aids' reads as helpers of a fitter, but the two words are simply the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Stratified describes rock, society or soil arranged in distinct strata, one level stacked above another.

clue.text: Series of earthquakes in sierra close to end

indicators.note: placing a word at the end tells you it follows the first piece rather than leading

blocks.note: Sierra is the NATO alphabet word for S
close weather is warm and muggy

explanation.surface: A run of tremors in the mountains is nearly over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sierra' looks like a mountain range but is the radio alphabet letter; 'close' is the weather sense, not 'near'.
explanation.definitionFit: Seismologists call a cluster of many small tremors with no main shock an earthquake swarm.

clue.text: Dressing I changed for lack of flexibility

indicators.note: what is changed has been altered, so these letters come out in a different order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone swapped a stiff bandage because it would not bend.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a wound dressing being replaced; the word is only letters to reorder.
explanation.definitionFit: Stiffness or inability to bend is the quality of being rigid, a straightforward noun synonym.

clue.text: Add small amount of alcohol, mostly ale

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: a tot is a small measure of spirits
taken as written before trimming

explanation.surface: A barman topping up a pint of beer with a shot of spirits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Add' looks like an instruction to mix the drinks, but it is the definition, used as a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To total a column of figures is to sum them, so the verbs are synonyms in arithmetic.

clue.text: Company cut down tree

indicators.note: cutting something down shortens it, so the last letter is lopped off

blocks.note: a firm is a business company

explanation.surface: A logging business felled a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut down' fits the logging picture perfectly, but it is shortening the word for a business.
explanation.definitionFit: The fir is a common evergreen conifer, a straightforward example of the general class.

clue.text: Looks at stuff from mine? Not a good sight

blocks.note: to eye something is to look at it
ore is the rock dug from a mine

explanation.surface: Someone inspects the spoil heaps from a mine and finds them ugly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mine' could be the possessive pronoun; here it is the pit.
explanation.definitionFit: An eyesore is something unpleasant to look at, such as an ugly building spoiling a view.

clue.text: Ten campers on the rocks forming steep hillside

indicators.note: something on the rocks is wrecked and broken up, so the letters are scattered into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A group of ten campers pitched on a rocky, steep slope.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the rocks' fits the hillside scene literally, which hides its role as the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: An escarpment is a long steep slope or cliff at the edge of a plateau or ridge.

clue.text: Performed a song including line in informal speech

indicators.note: to include something is to take it inside, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: past tense of sing
L is the standard abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: A singer slipped a casual spoken line into the performance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Line' is one of the commonest single-letter abbreviations, L, and it slots inside the past tense of the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang is the colloquial, non-standard vocabulary people use in casual conversation rather than formal writing.

clue.text: Weapon forming part of revolutionary multimode protection

indicators.note: what forms part of a phrase is a run of letters lying inside it
a revolution turns things round, so the letters are read backwards

blocks.note: the letters spanning the end of the first word and start of the second

explanation.surface: A rebel group's armour that guards against many kinds of attack includes a weapon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' reads as describing rebels, but it says to read the hidden run backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A torpedo is a self-propelled underwater missile fired from submarines or ships at targets.

clue.text: Destroy old book, well-read

blocks.note: O is the standard abbreviation for old
B is the abbreviation for book
a well-read person is literate

explanation.surface: An instruction to ruin an old volume that has been read many times.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Well-read' suggests a battered book, but it describes an educated person.
explanation.definitionFit: To obliterate is to wipe out or demolish completely, leaving no trace, so it matches destroying.

clue.text: SA animal or llama I’d disturbed

indicators.note: disturbed things are thrown into disorder, so these letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: Someone confesses to upsetting a South American creature, or perhaps a llama.
explanation.walkthrough: SA stands for South America here. The llama is also from that continent, which makes it feel like the answer, but it is only letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The armadillo is an armoured mammal native to South and Central America, an example of such a creature.

clue.text: Get contractors to do exterior to home before spring

indicators.note: coming before means placed first in the line, ahead of the next piece

blocks.note: someone not at home is out
a spring is the source of a river

explanation.surface: A homeowner hires builders to paint the outside of the house before spring arrives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spring' looks like the season, but it is the water source.
explanation.definitionFit: A company outsources work by paying an outside supplier to perform it rather than doing it in-house.

clue.text: Aid to smooth running regularly used in socials

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is kept

blocks.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: Something that keeps parties and gatherings going smoothly is often present at them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smooth running' sounds social, like a good host; the answer is the lubricant for machinery.
explanation.definitionFit: Oil lubricates an engine's moving parts so they turn freely with little friction.

clue.text: Said what to do to suitcase and a lot of money

indicators.note: said means spoken, so the phrase is to be heard rather than read

blocks.note: you pack a suitcase before a trip

explanation.surface: Instructions for getting ready for a trip and bringing plenty of cash.
explanation.walkthrough: In British informal speech a packet is a large sum, as in 'cost a packet'.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang uses this word for a large amount of money, as in saying a holiday cost a fortune.

clue.text: Inferior horse in mind for slaughter

indicators.note: something in another sits within it, so one piece goes inside

blocks.note: to mind is to care
a nag is a broken-down old horse

explanation.surface: A poor-quality horse is earmarked for the knacker's yard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mind' looks like a noun for thoughts, but it is the verb meaning to care.
explanation.definitionFit: Carnage is the large-scale killing of many people or animals, as in a massacre or battle.

clue.text: Confirm where English cricket fans will be?

definitions.text: where English cricket fans will be
definitions.note: a phrase (two words) rather than a verb

blocks.note: first meaning: to bear witness or certify

blocks.clueFragment: where English cricket fans will be
blocks.note: second meaning, split in two: present at a Test, an international cricket match

explanation.walkthrough: A Test is a multi-day international cricket match, so supporters will be 'at Test'. The question mark flags the playful second reading.
explanation.definitionFit: To attest is to declare or provide evidence that something is true, as a witness confirms a signature.

clue.text: What’s in piece arranged for organ

indicators.note: what lies within a phrase is a run of letters sitting inside it

blocks.note: the last letter of the first word and the first two of the second

explanation.surface: Asking what a composition scored for church organ contains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arranged' and 'organ' suggest music and even an anagram, but the answer simply sits across the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: The ear is the body's organ of hearing and balance, an example of a sensory organ.

clue.text: Champion drink, beer

blocks.note: to sup is to drink in small mouthfuls
porter is a dark beer

explanation.surface: Praise for an excellent beverage: a great beer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Champion' reads as an adjective praising the beer, but it is a noun for an advocate.
explanation.definitionFit: A champion of a cause is someone who backs and argues for it, a backer or advocate.

clue.text: Like some bears primarily placing our lives at risk

indicators.note: primarily means in the first place, so each word gives its opening letter

blocks.note: first letters of the five words

explanation.surface: Certain bears are a danger to human life.
explanation.walkthrough: The polar bear is the most dangerous bear to people, so the wordplay doubles as a fact about the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Polar is the adjective naming the white Arctic species, the polar bear, so it describes some bears.

clue.text: Health food

blocks.note: first meaning: a drink raised to someone's good health
second meaning: browned slices of bread

explanation.walkthrough: Read together, the two words suggest something nourishing; apart, one is a salute with a glass and the other grilled bread.
explanation.definitionFit: Raising glasses and saying 'your health' is drinking a toast, and toasted bread is everyday breakfast fare.

clue.text: Country path involves a very painful effort

indicators.note: to involve is to wrap up within, so one piece is enclosed by the other

blocks.note: a trail is a rough path through countryside
taken as written
V is the abbreviation for very

explanation.surface: Hiking a rural track turns out to be extremely hard work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very' looks like it intensifies 'painful', so the definition seems to be 'very painful effort'; the word is V inside the path.
explanation.definitionFit: Travail is archaic or literary for arduous, exhausting labour, and also the pains of childbirth.

clue.text: Fit a part

blocks.note: taken as written
PT is the abbreviation for part

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fit' reads as a verb, as in fitting a component; it is the adjective meaning suitable.
explanation.definitionFit: Something apt is suitable or appropriate for the occasion, the adjective sense of fitting.

clue.text: Respond about wandering cat

indicators.note: wandering things stray from their place, so the letters drift into a new order

blocks.note: re is Latin for concerning or about
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone is asked to reply regarding a stray cat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' is often RE in crosswords, from the Latin used in business letters ('re your enquiry').
explanation.definitionFit: To react is to do or say something in reply to a stimulus, a direct synonym for answering.

clue.text: Improvement of gambler chaps with time

blocks.note: one who bets
chaps are men
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Gamblers' lives improve as they grow older.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chaps' is the informal British word for men.
explanation.definitionFit: Betterment is making something or someone better, so it is a synonym for advancement or progress.
